Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself, typically with a smaller or simpler version of the same problem. Every recursive function needs a **base case**—a condition that stops the calling—so it doesn't repeat forever. Each call breaks the problem down a little more, working its way toward that base case. A classic example is `factorial(n) = n × factorial(n-1)`, where the base case is `factorial(0) = 1`.
